BlackRock Chief Investment Officer Rick Rieder warns that the $40 trillion national debt is a mounting fiscal burden, yet he views a 5% yield on 10-year Treasury bonds as a distinct buying opportunity for investors.

A Costly Fiscal Burden

Rieder told CNBC that Federal Reserve rate hikes carry immediate and severe fiscal consequences for the country. He noted that for every 100-basis-point increase in rates, the federal government faces an additional $100 billion in interest expense.

This dynamic creates a structural macroeconomic hurdle. “We’re going to have a compounding debt problem in the country,” Rieder stated, stressing that rates must ultimately fall to manage the nation’s soaring debt load.

Read Also: NVDA Is Booming, But BlackRock Sounds the Alarm on a $100 Billion AI Debt Problem: Are AI Bottleneck Plays BE, VRT, MU the Next Winners?

Seizing Fixed Income Opportunities

Despite these systemic fiscal concerns, the current bond market presents a rare entry point. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield recently surged to around 5.041% on Monday, Sept. 14, hitting a 19-year high not seen since July 2007. Reflecting on 10-year Treasury yields reaching 5%, Rieder emphasized the historical advantage for fixed-income buyers.

“95% of the time in history, when it does, it’s really good forward investment environment,” he said. While BlackRock remains significantly underweight on the back end of the yield curve due to supply pressures, Rieder admitted the firm has started “dabbling” by purchasing long-term Treasuries.

However, Rieder sees the most immediate value at the very front of the yield curve. He highlighted BlackRock’s short-duration ETF strategy, which achieves a 7.2% yield with an A- average rating while maintaining a duration of under three years.

Downgraded Equities and Rising Risks

The emergence of compelling fixed-income yields has shifted Rieder’s asset allocation strategy. He downgraded his outlook on U.S. equities to a “B minus,” a sharp contrast from the optimal environment he cited a year prior.

Because institutional investors can now secure their necessary 7% target returns through stable, low-volatility bonds, he noted that the “alternative to stocks is real.”

Finally, Rieder cautioned that higher real rates are generating systemic friction. He explicitly flagged a looming “rollover financing risk” for sectors dependent on leverage, pointing to real estate and bilateral credit finance as areas facing serious refinancing hurdles.

How Have Stocks and Bonds Performed in 2026?

At the last check, the 30-year Treasury bond yielded 5.36%, the 10-year Treasury bond was at 4.99%, and the two-year bond was at 4.65%.

The primary ETF specifically tracking the long end of the U.S. Treasury yield curve—including the 30-year benchmark bond—is the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ:TLT), which closed 0.27% lower at $80.71 on Tuesday. It was down 8.14% year-to-date, down 1.62% over the last month and 10.48% over the last year.

The S&P 500 index has advanced 10.60% year-to-date. Similarly, the Nasdaq Composite index was up 11.82%, and the Dow Jones gained 7.67% YTD.

On Tuesday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (NASDAQ:QQQ), which track the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100, respectively, closed lower. SPY fell 0.46% to $757.39, while QQQ fell 0.65% to $704.54. Meanwhile, the Dow tracker, State Street SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (NYSE:DIA), also ended 0.62% lower at $521.23.

In premarket on Wednesday, SPY was up 0.23%, QQQ gained 0.46% and DIA advanced 0.15%.

In the upcoming battle for Congress, a significant number of America’s wealthiest donors are reportedly throwing their weight behind the Republican Party.

Out of the 20 top donors in the U.S.,16 are backing the Republican campaign, with George Soros being a prominent Democratic supporter. Some of these mega-donors are supporting candidates who favor deregulation of cryptocurrency and gambling, or the advancement of AI, according to the Financial Times on Wednesday.

“What you’re seeing is a mild break from expectations,” Stanford political scientist Adam Bonica told the publication. He observed that while it’s not uncommon for leading donors to favor Republicans, the balance in this election is “especially skewed”.

Over a third of the $2.8 billion raised for the 2025-26 election cycle is from the 20 largest mega-donors, as per the report. “We now have a system that is geared towards and depends on these ultra-wealthy mega-donors,” stated Brendan Glavin, research director at OpenSecrets.

Citadel CEO Ken Griffin has also backed Republican candidates through multiple political groups, including organizations supporting races in Wyoming and Tennessee, while contributing about one-third of a group’s funding opposing Alaska Democratic challenger, the report stated.

Read Also: Trump Says It's 'Easy' to Handle $5,000 Payments if Republicans Win 2026 Midterms: 'We're Taking in So Much Money'

Crypto Donors Build Political War Chest

Notable contributions have also come from special interest groups. Crypto entrepreneurs Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss donated approximately $11 million, while tech giants Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz and their spouses have contributed $18 million. OpenAI Co-Founder Greg Brockman and his spouse donated $25 million, the report added.

The cryptocurrency industry has built one of the largest political war chests of the election, backing candidates who support the sector. Crypto super PAC Fairshake has raised more than $99 million in individual contributions, with nearly all of the funding coming from a handful of companies and investors, including Coinbase Global Inc. (NASDAQ:COIN), Ripple, Andreessen and Horowitz.

GOP Midterm Cash Gets Musk, Trump Boost

Earlier this month, House Speaker Mike Johnson‘s meeting with billionaire Elon Musk sparked speculation about potential financial backing for the GOP’s midterm campaign, adding to the momentum.

Musk donated more than $250 million to President Donald Trump’s 2024 re-election campaign and is reportedly planning to spend over $100 million on the 2026 midterms, potentially supporting House Republicans through his America PAC.

Meanwhile, Trump said he plans to spend a large portion of MAGA Inc.’s roughly $850 million war chest to support Republican candidates in the 2026 midterms, along with some of his own funds. “We’re in very good shape,” said the President.

Big Tech Prepares For Midterm Shift

A report in August, however, stated that companies previously aligned closely with Trump are strengthening ties with Democrats as they hedge against a possible change in House control after the 2026 midterms.

Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) reportedly is making sizable donations to Democrats, while Paramount Skydance (NASDAQ:PSKY) and Kalshi are hiring former Democratic aides for government relations.

Big tech firms including Meta and Palantir Technologies Inc.(NASDAQ:PLTR) are also preparing for possible congressional information requests, hearings, and potential subpoenas tied to their Trump-era involvement.

The AI spending boom has become two things at once. It is the trade investors are most sure about, and the place they think a credit accident is most likely to start.

In Bank of America’s September Global Fund Manager Survey, 53% named buying global semiconductor stocks the most crowded trade in the market.

A crowded trade is one nearly everyone already owns, which is what makes it fragile when sentiment turns.

In the same survey, 42% named AI infrastructure spending the most likely source of a systemic credit event, up from 38% in August.

Government debt ranked second at 25% and private credit third at 19%.

Both answers describe the same money.

AI Spending Still Has Believers

BofA Global Research said in the survey that "investor conviction on macro boom and fast-paced AI capex is still strong."

The survey ran Sept. 4-10 among 190 managers overseeing $512 billion.

A growing 79% of respondents expect no AI infrastructure spender to announce a spending cut this year, up from 71% in August.

For equipment suppliers, that is a demand forecast.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) shows why. Its data center revenue reached $89 billion in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, up 117% from a year earlier.

The company also forecast $108 billion in total revenue for the following quarter.

The five largest spenders, Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL), are on track for roughly $700 billion of capital expenditures in 2026.

Analysts at Bank of America and Evercore project the figure passes $1 trillion in 2027.

Read Also: How Many Rate Hikes Will The Fed Deliver In This Cycle? Economists Answer

The Supplier’s Revenue Is The Customer’s Bill

Nvidia’s sales are its customers’ outlays. Strong chip demand proves the equipment is wanted. It does not prove each buyer earns a return on it.

Oracle is where that gap is most visible.

In its results released earlier this month, the company reported $28.5 billion of capital spending in a single quarter and negative free cash flow of $5.4 billion, partly covered by a $20 billion at-the-market equity sale.

Full-year capex guidance is $90 billion to $95 billion, and management gave no date for a return to positive free cash flow.

A record net 33% of survey respondents said companies are overinvesting.

"AI hyperscaler capex continues to be seen as the most likely source of a systemic credit event (per 42%)," said analyst Michael Hartnett.

That 42% reading increased from 38% in August, exceeding government debt at 25% and private credit at 19%.

The Credit Market Is Already Separating The Two

On Wednesday, Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok added evidence from credit markets: investors are paying more to protect against hyperscaler defaults while bank protection costs remain stable.

Five-year CDS on a basket of Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Oracle has climbed above 100 basis points, the highest in Slok’s eight-year series.

The equivalent contracts on JPMorgan Chase & Co., Citigroup Inc., Bank of America Corp., Wells Fargo & Co. and U.S. Bancorp have sat flat near 40 basis points.

A credit default swap, or CDS, is insurance on a company’s bonds. A rising premium means lenders want more money to carry the same risk.

“The widening in hyperscaler CDS is not driven by dealer hedging of new issuance,” Slok said.

According to Slok, this is driven by a debt-financed spending cycle with rising leverage, negative free cash flow, and an uncertain payback on assets that lose value over time.

"The widening in hyperscaler CDS is not driven by dealer hedging of new issuance," Slok said.

The five hyperscalers sold about $121 billion in U.S. investment-grade bonds in 2025, compared with an average of roughly $28 billion per year from 2020 to 2024, according to Bank of America.

By midsummer 2026, issuance had passed $180 billion.

A Federal Reserve rate hike is largely priced in for Wednesday, but JPMorgan says the S&P 500 could still swing anywhere from 1% higher to 2% lower depending on how Chair Kevin Warsh frames the move.

A surprise decision to hold rates steady could prove painful. JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE:JPM) estimates the index could fall 1.25% to 1.75% if the Fed leaves rates unchanged.

Why a Hold Could Hurt Stocks

Polymarket traders put the chance of a 25-basis-point hike at 89% Wednesday morning, compared with 11% for no change, with roughly $193 million traded on the decision.

JPMorgan argues that an unexpected hold could raise doubts about the Fed’s willingness to contain inflation, potentially pushing longer-term Treasury yields higher as investors demand more compensation for inflation risk.

That matters with the 10-year Treasury yield around 5%. Reuters reported Wednesday that investors are increasingly focused on whether Warsh can reinforce the Fed’s inflation-fighting credibility.

JPMorgan Maps Five Outcomes

JPMorgan sees a surprise hold sending the S&P 500 down 1.25% to 1.75%.

A 25-basis-point hike with little guidance could instead lift the index 0.25% to 0.75%.

The bank’s most bullish scenario is a hike accompanied by a signal that the Fed is simply unwinding the 75 basis points of easing delivered in 2025. JPMorgan sees the S&P rising 0.5% to 1%.

Stocks could fall 0.25% to 1% if Warsh signals the Fed may need to keep rates higher for longer than investors currently expect.

In the most bearish case, Warsh signals rates need to rise materially further to bring inflation under control, and JPMorgan sees a 1% to 2% decline.

The August Consumer Price Index report shows a 0.4% monthly increase, prompting Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at the Carson Group, to warn that the U.S. economy faces “stickier inflation.” He argues that broad cost increases across services demonstrate that recent price spikes are not “a one-time event.”

The ‘Sticky’ Reality

Evaluating the data alongside Chief Macro Strategist Sonu Varghese, Detrick challenged the narrative that specific price increases are temporary anomalies.

He emphasized that writing off categories like wireless plans, airfare, or lodging as outliers ignores the underlying trend keeping prices elevated.

Detrick specifically called out the rising costs of pet care, bluntly labeling vet bills a “money pit” for consumers. Because costs are rising across the board, Detrick concluded that the economy is experiencing “stickier inflation” rather than isolated shocks.

Read Also: Ex-Fed Economist Warns About ‘Inflation Trap’ As Central Bank Prepares to Vote

Services Driving the Surge

Service-level inflation remains a primary driver of the core advances. The official CPI data shows airline fares surged 23.4% over the last year. The shelter index increased by 3.0% annually, while the lodging away from home index rose 2.4% in August alone.

With essential services continuing to climb, Detrick noted that corporate profits are also benefiting from the pressure. He observed that “one person’s inflation is another company’s margin expansion,” indicating that these price levels may remain entrenched in the economy.

Breaking Down the CPI Data

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the all items index rose 3.4% for the 12 months ending in August. The core index, which excludes food and energy, increased 0.3% over the month and 2.4% annually.

Energy proved to be a significant factor in the headline number. The overall energy index rose 2.1% in August, driven by a 3.9% increase in the gasoline index. Over the past 12 months, the energy index has increased 16.3%, while the food index has risen 2.7%.

How Have Stock Markets Performed in 2026?

The S&P 500 index has advanced 10.60% year-to-date. Similarly, the Nasdaq Composite index was up 11.82%, and the Dow Jones gained 7.67% YTD.

Nvidia Corp’s (NASDAQ:NVDA) AI expansion is reaching a part of the technology stack investors rarely associate with GPUs: the radio network. Nokia Corp (NYSE:NOK) says eight global telecom operators are now advancing AI-RAN trials using its platform and Nvidia technology, suggesting the AI infrastructure boom could eventually extend beyond data centers and into the cell towers connecting billions of devices.

AI Moves Into RAN

Nokia said Wednesday that A1 Group, Chunghwa Telecom, du, e&, Mobily, stc, TPG Telecom and Zain Saudi are advancing proofs of concept and live field trials using Nokia’s AI-native radio access network (AI-RAN) platform powered by Nvidia’s Aerial RAN Computer. The trials span Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East.

The underlying idea is relatively simple: use AI and accelerated computing to make wireless networks more efficient. Nokia says its AI-RAN platform has already demonstrated more than 20% spectral-efficiency gains, with advanced AI models targeting more than 2x efficiency over time. Higher spectral efficiency means operators can move more data through the spectrum they already own, potentially increasing network capacity without relying solely on additional spectrum or hardware.

That is where Nvidia enters the picture. Nokia combines its anyRAN software with Nvidia accelerated computing to run AI models at radio-network timescales. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has described the radio access network as "the next AI infrastructure," framing the opportunity as a shift from using AI to simply optimize networks toward making the network itself an AI computing platform.

See More: Top Momentum Stocks

Nokia Wants AI at the Edge

For Nokia, AI-RAN could turn its existing network footprint into a software-driven growth opportunity.

The company’s AI-native RAN platform, powered by Nvidia computing, is expected to begin pilots later this year and reach commercial availability in 2027.

Nokia also sees the technology as a path from 5G and 5G-Advanced toward AI-native 6G.

Nvidia’s AI Footprint Expands

The bigger investor implication may be for Nvidia.

The company has built its AI dominance around data-center computing, but AI-RAN opens another potential layer of demand: the telecommunications network itself. Nokia brings the radio expertise and operator relationships, while NVIDIA supplies accelerated computing and AI software.

The commercial opportunity is still developing. Today’s operator trials must ultimately demonstrate that the additional computing produces enough network capacity and economic value to justify deployment at scale.

But the direction is becoming clearer. As AI workloads spread from centralized data centers toward the network edge, Nokia is positioning its radio business to become part of Nvidia’s expanding AI infrastructure ecosystem — and cell towers could become another place where GPUs matter.

Independent AI research firm SemiAnalysis argues making increasingly powerful models safer may itself consume substantial computing power, which may calm fears that Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) may face the fallout from slower artificial intelligence development.

Safety Work Eats Compute

Speaking on SemiAnalysis’s podcast Tuesday, analyst Max Kan said the market may be overlooking two factors.

First, AI companies still want more computing capacity than can physically come online.

“Demand will continue to outstrip supply,” Kan said.

Second, safety itself requires compute. AI labs increasingly use models to monitor other models, test safeguards and check the reinforcement-learning environments used to improve their systems.

Kan said people “underestimate how much compute is required for safety, alignment” and monitoring. He also pointed to interpretability, research aimed at understanding how models reach their answers, as another compute-intensive workload.

Another host said the “nuanced take” is that labs could actually “spend a lot more compute” as they devote more resources to making increasingly capable systems safer.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has made a similar point. His proposal to pace frontier AI does not call for halting training, but for devoting more resources to alignment, interpretability, testing and operational safeguards.

Cybersecurity Cuts Both Ways

SemiAnalysis also argued that advanced AI could reshape cybersecurity by forcing companies to fight AI with AI.

The panel pointed to Greg Brockman’s description of a continuous security system at OpenAI that would use the latest models to constantly find and patch vulnerabilities. As attackers deploy autonomous agents at scale, defenders may need equally capable AI systems running continuously to detect and stop them.

One speaker called it potentially “the most impactful shift in cybersecurity,” arguing that companies capable of delivering security outcomes rather than simply selling tools could capture enormous value.

The hosts warned that major cybersecurity firms could themselves become prime targets for increasingly capable AI attacks, naming Okta Inc. (NASDAQ:OKTA), CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWD), Palo Alto Networks Inc. (NASDAQ:PANW) and Zscaler Inc. (NASDAQ:ZS).

Near-Term Pause Still Bites

OpenAI paused frontier reinforcement-learning training after its Hugging Face incident, and its largest planned frontier run remains on hold while smaller training and evaluations continue.

President Donald Trump on Monday called fears of runaway AI a “hoax” and questioned why an industry would seek rules that could bankrupt it.

Polymarket traders give a U.S. AI safety law a 16% chance of passing before 2027, with about $123,000 traded. The contract covers measures including restrictions on AI training or use and requirements for human oversight.

For Nvidia, the question is whether slower frontier training cuts more GPU demand than safety, monitoring and cybersecurity add back. Shares recovered 0.6% Tuesday.

The biggest threat to Nvidia Corp’s (NASDAQ:NVDA) AI boom may not be a slowdown in demand. It may be whether the power grid can keep up. As Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang pushes back against calls to slow AI development, Nvidia is simultaneously working with Alphabet Inc‘s (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOG) Google and energy companies to make AI data centers flexible enough to respond to grid conditions — revealing the infrastructure constraint behind the next phase of the boom.

Nvidia Rejects AI Slowdown

The debate over AI’s pace intensified this week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei renewed calls for the industry to slow frontier AI development and strengthen safety measures. Huang took the opposite view at Salesforce, Inc.‘s (NYSE:CRM) Dreamforce conference, arguing that AI safety should be treated primarily as an engineering challenge rather than a reason to slow development.

That matters for Nvidia because its business depends on the continued expansion of AI computing infrastructure. Every new generation of models and AI agents requires more computing, and that computing ultimately requires electricity.

Huang has increasingly framed energy as part of the AI infrastructure equation. Nvidia’s recent work focuses on getting more AI output from each unit of electricity, rather than treating power availability as a fixed constraint. Its DSX platform is designed to coordinate compute, networking, cooling and power so AI factories can produce more tokens per watt.

See More: Top Growth Stocks

AI Data Centers Meet The Grid

That strategy took a bigger step Wednesday.

Nvidia, Google and Emerald AI launched the AI Energy Management Alliance, Axios reported. The alliance brings together 18 companies across AI, utilities and energy. The group wants to make data centers flexible enough to adjust electricity consumption in response to grid conditions, potentially allowing more AI capacity to connect without overwhelming local power systems.

The idea is not to make AI use less power in absolute terms. It is to make the demand more flexible.

Nvidia says Emerald AI has demonstrated data centers reducing power demand by as much as 40% in under a minute while maintaining critical workloads. The company says that flexibility could help unlock up to 100 gigawatts of existing U.S. grid capacity for AI factories.

That could become increasingly important as AI data centers grow larger and compete with households, manufacturers and other industries for scarce grid capacity.

Power Becomes The Bottleneck

For Nvidia investors, this creates an unusual tension.

The company is arguing that AI development should continue rapidly, while simultaneously investing in technology designed to manage one of the physical limits to that expansion.

That doesn’t mean electricity demand will slow Nvidia’s growth. Instead, it suggests the company’s opportunity is expanding into another layer of the AI stack: helping data centers manage the power needed to run Nvidia’s own GPUs.

The next phase of the AI infrastructure race may therefore be measured not just in GPUs, racks or data centers, but in megawatts that can actually reach them. If Nvidia can help customers turn power-hungry AI factories into flexible grid assets, electricity will no longer be just a constraint on AI growth and will become another infrastructure market Nvidia can help optimize.

Cathie Wood says SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) had no need for public markets as long as Starlink kept generating cash. Elon Musk’s push into orbital AI data centers changed that.

"I never thought SpaceX would go public," the ARK Invest CEO told Livewire. "Then Elon decided to get into orbital data centers."

"He needs so much capital," Wood said. "He needs the scaling that the public equity markets will provide."

The Numbers Behind Wood’s Argument

SpaceX’s financials help explain her thinking. Its Connectivity business, primarily Starlink, generated $4.42 billion in operating income in 2025, while its AI business lost $6.36 billion.

The equation changed further when SpaceX acquired Musk’s xAI in February, bringing the Grok developer and its expensive data-center buildout inside SpaceX.

SpaceX raised about $85.7 billion in its June IPO and told investors the proceeds would help fund AI compute infrastructure alongside launch systems and satellite capacity. AI capital spending then reached $15.83 billion in the second quarter, about 86% of total quarterly capex, according to company filings.

SpaceX has not said orbital data centers were the reason for the IPO, but the company’s spending shows how sharply AI changed its capital needs.

Can Orbit Solve AI’s Data Center Problem?

SpaceX argues orbital computing could avoid some constraints facing terrestrial AI data centers, including access to electricity, land, cooling water and increasingly restrictive permitting and regulation, by tapping solar energy in orbit. The economics, however, depend heavily on Starship making it cheap enough to launch enormous amounts of computing hardware.

Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) offers a useful warning. Its Project Natick was a technical success: Microsoft said servers in its underwater data center failed at just one-eighth the rate of a comparable land-based system.

But Microsoft never scaled Natick into a commercial business. Customers preferred conventional data centers that were cheaper and easier to expand and upgrade, while the sealed design made replacing rapidly improving AI chips difficult, people familiar with the project told Reuters.

Prediction traders remain skeptical about how quickly the concept can reach meaningful scale. Kalshi puts the chance of a 1-megawatt orbital data center going live before 2031 at 30%, with $46,000 traded on the market.

Musk is pushing a much faster timetable. He said he is "highly confident" SpaceX will launch AI computers from Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) into orbit in 2027, with "significant" scale expected in 2028.

The project would extend Apple’s chip strategy beyond consumer devices. Apple recently refreshed its Mac lineup with M6, M5 Pro, M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, saying the 2-nanometer M6 delivers up to four times faster AI performance.

The server initiative reportedly began about a year ago with backing from current CEO John Ternus.

Apple does not expect a launch before 2029, and the project could still be canceled or proceed without NVIDIA technology.

If launched, it would mark Apple’s first dedicated server hardware since it discontinued Xserve in 2011.

Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) could emerge as a key beneficiary as AI spending shifts from training models toward running large-scale inference workloads.

Lip Favors Broadcom For Inference

BakerAvenue Wealth Management chief strategist King Lip said Nvidia has excelled in AI model training. But for large, repetitive inference workloads, Broadcom is Lip’s “top pick” for the next evolution in custom AI chips and inference play.

He added that Broadcom doesn’t need Nvidia to lose market share to expand, as both companies can benefit from different parts of growing AI infrastructure demand.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) has gained after only two of the past 14 Fed decisions, yet one analyst argues a surprise today could make it three.

What the Consensus Expects

As Benzinga reported Wednesday, Polymarket traders price a 25-basis-point hike at 89% with roughly $193 million traded on the decision. 

JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM) mapped out five scenarios for what happens next, with a surprise hold seen as the most painful outcome for stocks, potentially sending the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) down 1.25% to 1.75%. 

What Warsh says at the 2:30 p.m. ET press conference matters more than the hike itself, according to the bank.

Why the Press Conference Could Backfire

Macro analyst Robin Brooks wrote in a Substack post Wednesday that Warsh faces an impossible task. 

Markets price not just today’s hike but another 25 basis points by December and two more in 2027. Since Warsh has a well-known aversion to forward guidance, the press conference will almost certainly sound dovish relative to what markets want. 

Brooks’ base case lands in the “dovish hike” bucket, triggering curve steepening, a weaker dollar, and gold moving higher. He called it the same trap Warsh fell into at the July meeting.

The Contrarian Bitcoin Case

On-chain analyst Ali Martinez posted a thread on X Wednesday, arguing that if Warsh surprises with a hold, the shock could trigger a powerful rally across risk assets. 

Bitcoin has gained after only two of the past 14 FOMC decisions, and a no-hike outcome could push it from $75,000 back above $82,000 as investors rapidly reposition. 

Ali Martinez framed it as a political calculation: Trump needs a win before the midterms, and another rate hike adds economic pressure heading into November.

The contrarian case sits against 89% market odds and the CLARITY Act’s failure Tuesday, which removed one of Bitcoin’s two main near-term catalysts. 

What Warsh says after the hike, rather than the hike itself, looks like the key variable for crypto markets heading into Wednesday afternoon.
